title: Diverse Histories and Common Origins of Nitrogen-enhanced JWST Galaxies
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures. Submitted. Comments are welcome
summary: Early JWST spectra revealed galaxies with a strong nitrogen excess challenging galactic chemical evolution models. Using public JWST surveys, we construct a sample of 76 N/O-enhanced galaxies (NOEGs) at 4 $<z<$ 8.5, the largest at high redshift to date. The NOEG fraction rises from $\sim$3% to $\sim$18% between $z\sim$ 4 and 7 - well above the $\sim$2% measured locally - potentially driven by burstier, cluster-dominated star formation. Stacked spectra of the most nitrogen-rich galaxies show signatures of low-metallicity Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars, a likely source of primary nitrogen within the first few Myr of a starburst, with UV and optical continua dominated by young stellar emission and Balmer jumps evident in some cases. Many NOEGs also exhibit ionised outflows: 40% show secondary [O III] and H$α$ components, while stacked spectra of the remainder reveal a broadened, offset H$α$ without forbidden-line counterparts, suggesting dust-attenuated or faded outflows. The continuum in the latter shows a weak Balmer break, indicating these galaxies are past their most recent burst. This suggests that outflows dilute gas metallicity after the first few Myr of the initial enrichment and enable renewed N/O enhancement driven by low-metallicity Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars. We conclude that NOEGs are caught briefly after a recent starburst: either within $\sim$10 Myr, when WR winds drive nitrogen enrichment, or after 30-40 Myr, when AGB winds take over - following an outflow driven by radiative or supernova feedback, consistent with recent chemical evolution models.

AI.tldr: JWST reveals N/O-enhanced galaxies at z~4-8.5, with fraction rising from ~3% to ~18%. These galaxies show Wolf-Rayet signatures (primary N source in <10 Myr) or AGB-driven enrichment (30-40 Myr) after outflow dilution, consistent with bursty, cluster-dominated star formation.
AI.motivation: Early JWST spectra uncovered galaxies with unexpectedly strong nitrogen excess that challenge standard galactic chemical evolution models, motivating a systematic search and characterization of N/O-enhanced galaxies at high redshift.
AI.method: Constructed a sample of 76 N/O-enhanced galaxies (NOEGs) at 4<z<8.5 from public JWST surveys. Analyzed stacked spectra for Wolf-Rayet signatures, Balmer jumps, ionized outflows, and stellar continuum properties. Compared NOEG fraction evolution with local measurements.
AI.result: NOEG fraction rises from ~3% at z~4 to ~18% at z~7 (vs ~2% locally). Two populations identified: (1) young starbursts (<10 Myr) with WR winds producing primary nitrogen; (2) older systems (30-40 Myr) with AGB-driven enrichment after outflow dilution. 40% show ionized outflows with secondary components.
AI.conclusion: NOEGs are transient post-starburst phases caught briefly after recent enrichment events. Nitrogen enhancement proceeds in two stages: early WR-driven (<10 Myr) and later AGB-driven (30-40 Myr) after feedback-driven outflows dilute the gas, consistent with bursty chemical evolution models.

title: Compact Core, Extended Reach: A Bipolar kpc-Scale Elongation in a Little Red Dot at $z \approx 5.5$
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) appear extremely compact at rest-frame optical wavelengths, yet many show extended rest-frame UV morphology revealing more complex internal structure. We present a combined analysis of VLT/MUSE rest-frame UV integral-field spectroscopy and continuum-subtracted [O III], H$β$, and H$α$+[N II] emission-line maps from JWST/NIRCam imaging at sub-kpc resolution for LRD-204851 at $z=5.482$ in GOODS-S. We find that LRD-204851 hosts a remarkably thin, bipolar, elongated structure passing through the optical continuum centroid and extending several kpc on either side, traced by both the UV continuum and the rest-frame optical emission lines, with a bright [O III] clump-like structure $\sim$2 kpc to the south-east of the centroid. The MUSE observations reveal a double-peaked Ly$α$ profile, with a broad and bright near-systemic red peak and a relatively faint peak blueshifted by $\sim$430 km s$^{-1}$, accompanied by a tentative N V $λ1238$ detection at similar velocity. In narrow-band imaging extracted from the MUSE IFU cube, both the blue Ly$α$ peak and the tentative N V emission lean toward this same south-eastern direction. Independently, radiative-transfer modeling of the integrated Ly$α$ profile favors a biconical low-column-density cavity in a dense, slowly expanding neutral envelope, in support of the bipolar geometry traced by the line maps. Together, these results suggest that the elongated emission of LRD-204851 is connected to radiation and/or gas flow from its central engine through a low-column-density channel with a small opening angle that may trace either a slow outflow or a quasi-static ionization cone. LRD-204851 is one of the first LRDs where the central engine's impact on its host galaxy is potentially directly observable on kpc scales.

AI.tldr: LRD-204851 at z=5.482 shows a thin, bipolar, kpc-scale elongated structure traced by UV continuum and optical emission lines, with double-peaked Lyα and tentative N V emission, consistent with a biconical low-column-density cavity from radiative-transfer modeling, suggesting direct kpc-scale influence of the central engine on the host galaxy.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal structure of Little Red Dots (LRDs), which appear compact at rest-frame optical but extended in UV, by investigating the connection between their central engines and host galaxy morphology at high spatial resolution.
AI.method: Combined analysis of VLT/MUSE rest-frame UV integral-field spectroscopy and JWST/NIRCam continuum-subtracted emission-line maps ([O III], Hβ, Hα+[N II]) at sub-kpc resolution, plus radiative-transfer modeling of the integrated Lyα profile.
AI.result: LRD-204851 hosts a thin, bipolar, elongated structure extending several kpc traced by UV continuum and optical emission lines, with a bright [O III] clump ~2 kpc SE of the centroid. MUSE reveals double-peaked Lyα (broad red peak, faint blue peak blueshifted by ~430 km/s) and tentative N V λ1238. Narrow-band imaging shows blue Lyα peak and N V emission leaning SE. Radiative-transfer modeling favors a biconical low-column-density cavity in a dense, slowly expanding neutral envelope.
AI.conclusion: The elongated emission likely arises from radiation/gas flow from the central engine through a low-column-density channel with small opening angle, possibly a slow outflow or quasi-static ionization cone, making LRD-204851 one of the first LRDs with directly observable kpc-scale central engine influence on its host.

title: A Long Period Stellar-Mass Black Hole Binary in $ω$ Centauri
comment: 23 pages, 9 figures; accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Modern simulations of stellar dynamics in globular clusters peg a dominant role for stellar-mass black holes, but direct evidence for black holes in clusters remains limited. We present the discovery of an astrometric stellar-mass black hole--main sequence star binary in $ω$ Centauri, the most massive Galactic globular cluster, using Hubble Space Telescope data from the oMEGACat project and additional JWST data that span a total of 23 years. The luminous companion to the black hole is a main-sequence turnoff star, and has a period of $94^{+63}_{-42}$ years, a semi-major axis of $31^{+15}_{-12}$ AU, and an eccentricity of $e=0.72^{+0.08}_{-0.13}$. Since we observe the binary during periastron, the mass of the black hole is well-constrained even though we only observe a partial orbit: the inferred black hole mass is $4.46^{+1.22}_{-1.01}$ M$_\odot$. We call this black hole oMEGACat BH-2. This is the first astrometric discovery of a stellar-mass black hole in a globular cluster, and is the longest period black hole binary system yet discovered. The low mass of this black hole is perhaps surprising given the low metallicity of the cluster, and shows that at least some low-mass black holes form at metallicity $Z<10^{-3}$. We find that the binary is almost certainly dynamically formed and is soft, with an expected binary disruption timescale of $\sim$800 Myr. While the total number of black hole binaries in $ω$ Centauri is uncertain, we show that existing surveys only cover a small area of parameter space, and that the presence of additional detectable black hole binaries is likely.

AI.tldr: Using 23 years of HST and JWST data, researchers discovered an astrometric stellar-mass black hole—main sequence star binary (oMEGACat BH-2) in ω Centauri, the most massive Galactic globular cluster. The black hole has a mass of 4.46 M☉, the companion is a main-sequence turnoff star with a 94-year period and high eccentricity (0.72). This is the first astrometric black hole discovery in a globular cluster and the longest period black hole binary known. The binary is dynamically formed, soft, and likely to disrupt in ~800 Myr.
AI.motivation: Stellar-mass black holes are predicted to be dominant in globular cluster dynamics, but direct observational evidence for black holes in clusters has been very limited. This discovery helps fill that gap.
AI.method: Astrometric analysis using HST data from the oMEGACat project and additional JWST data spanning 23 years, observing the binary during periastron to constrain the black hole mass despite only a partial orbit.
AI.result: Discovery of oMEGACat BH-2: a stellar-mass black hole (4.46 M☉) in a binary with a main-sequence turnoff star; period ~94 years, semi-major axis ~31 AU, eccentricity 0.72. First astrometric BH discovery in a globular cluster; longest period BH binary known.
AI.conclusion: Low-mass black holes can form at very low metallicity (Z<10⁻³). The binary is dynamically formed and soft, with ~800 Myr disruption timescale. Existing surveys cover limited parameter space, suggesting additional detectable black hole binaries likely exist in ω Centauri.

title: TNG SAM: Bridging Hydrodynamical Complexity and Semi-Analytic Efficiency to Model Galaxy Formation
summary: All cosmological models of galaxy formation must navigate the trade-off between physical accuracy and computational efficiency. Hydrodynamical simulations provide spatially resolved predictions for the co-evolution of dark matter, gas, stars, and black holes, but rely on phenomenological subgrid models for small-scale processes (e.g., star formation). Semi-analytic models (SAMs), by contrast, gain efficiency through simplified, analytic treatments of the same processes, at the cost of reduced predictive scope. In this work, we leverage the strengths of the Santa Cruz SAM and the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical simulation to develop the TNG SAM. Calibrated to reproduce baryon cycling in stellar feedback-dominated TNG galaxies ($\sim 10^{10}M_\odot < M_{200} < 10^{12}M_\odot$), the TNG SAM introduces several key updates to the Santa Cruz framework regarding: 1) halo gas (re-)accretion efficiency, 2) a cooling model that moves beyond the traditional cold/hot mode dichotomy, 3) explicit treatment of both galactic- and halo-scale outflows, 4) star formation efficiency, and 5) the circulation of metals between galaxies and their surroundings. These changes enable the TNG SAM to reproduce TNG's flow of gas and metals from the scale of the galaxy to the halo, as well as global galaxy (e.g., stellar mass) and halo (e.g. hot halo gas mass) properties within $\lesssim 30\%$ accuracy out to $z=6$. This work demonstrates that, with appropriate calibration, SAMs can capture the complex physics of galaxy formation modeled in hydrodynamical simulations while providing a flexible framework for studying galaxy evolution across the large cosmological volumes targeted by future observational surveys.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the TNG SAM, a semi-analytic model calibrated to reproduce baryon cycling and galaxy/halo properties from the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical simulation within ~30% accuracy out to z=6, bridging the gap between physical accuracy and computational efficiency in galaxy formation modeling.
AI.motivation: To bridge the trade-off between physical accuracy (hydrodynamical simulations) and computational efficiency (semi-analytic models) by developing a SAM that captures the complex physics of hydrodynamical simulations while enabling studies across large cosmological volumes.
AI.method: Calibrated the Santa Cruz SAM against the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical simulation, introducing five key updates: 1) halo gas (re-)accretion efficiency, 2) a cooling model beyond cold/hot mode dichotomy, 3) explicit treatment of galactic- and halo-scale outflows, 4) star formation efficiency, and 5) metal circulation between galaxies and their surroundings.
AI.result: The TNG SAM reproduces TNG's gas and metal flows from galaxy to halo scales, and matches global galaxy (stellar mass) and halo (hot gas mass) properties within ≤30% accuracy out to redshift z=6.
AI.conclusion: With appropriate calibration, SAMs can capture the complex physics modeled in hydrodynamical simulations and provide a flexible framework for studying galaxy evolution across large cosmological volumes targeted by future surveys.

title: Late-time JWST/NIRCam Observations of the Extremely Long-duration GRB 250702B/EP 250702a and Its Host Galaxy
summary: We present JWST/NIRCam observations of the extremely long-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) 250702B taken at ~ 95 days post-GRB (observer frame). The observations of the host galaxy reveal a single galaxy with a prominent dust lane observed nearly edge-on. Prospector modeling of the host galaxy photometry finds a high stellar mass (log(M_*/M_Sun) = 11.0 +0.2/-0.3) and large dust column (A_V = 2.8 +/- 0.3 mag), in agreement with previous results. If GRB 250702B is a collapsar-driven GRB, the host galaxy is the brightest (in rest-frame r and rest-frame H) and most massive compared to GRB hosts at similar redshifts. The transient localization is near the dust lane, and while we find no evidence for transient emission in F277W, F356W, and F444W, forced photometry in F150W and F200W reveals possible ~ 3 sigma detections of the transient at m_{F150W} ~ 27.9 AB mag and m_{F200W} ~ 27.4 AB mag. If these are secure detections, they are indicative of a late-time light curve flattening. This behavior is consistent with that of jetted tidal disruption events (TDEs); however, it is also consistent with a supernova plus GRB afterglow model. Alternatively, if these are upper limits, they are consistent with, but do not further constrain, the extrapolated power-law decline of the afterglow. The ambiguity of the possible detection of the transient in F150W and F200W highlights the need for late-time template observations with JWST/NIRCam.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRCam observations at ~95 days post-GRB of GRB 250702B reveal a massive, dusty, edge-on host galaxy (log M*/M☉ = 11.0). Possible ~3σ transient detections in F150W/F200W suggest late-time light curve flattening, consistent with either jetted TDEs or supernova+afterglow models, but upper limits cannot be ruled out.
AI.motivation: To characterize the host galaxy and late-time emission of the extremely long-duration GRB 250702B, testing whether its origin is a collapsar or a jetted tidal disruption event (TDE).
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam imaging at ~95 days post-GRB; Prospector SED modeling of host galaxy photometry; forced photometry at the transient location.
AI.result: Host is the brightest and most massive GRB host at similar redshifts (log M*/M☉ = 11.0, A_V = 2.8 mag). Possible ~3σ transient detections in F150W (27.9 AB) and F200W (27.4 AB) indicate late-time flattening; alternatively, these may be upper limits consistent with power-law afterglow decline.
AI.conclusion: The transient's late-time behavior is ambiguous—consistent with both jetted TDE and supernova+afterglow interpretations. Template observations are needed to resolve the nature of the emission.

title: The Lumina Project: Intergalactic Clumping and Recombination Sinks
comment: 23 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to OJA. Please visit https://lumina-simulation.com for more details
summary: Recombinations during the Epoch of Reionization are intrinsically inhomogeneous, with different regions of the intergalactic medium contributing unevenly depending on their density, temperature, ionization state, and spatial patchiness. We combine the high- and medium-resolution 95.5 cMpc Thesan-1 andh Thesan-2 runs with the significantly larger 500 cMpc Lumina simulation to measure clumping factors and recombination rates consistently across different resolutions and box sizes. We consider the standard ionized hydrogen clumping factor, $C_{\rm HII} \equiv \langle n_{\rm HII}^2\rangle/\langle n_{\rm HII}\rangle^2$, and a recombination-weighted clumping factor, $C_{\rm rec}$. Despite differences in resolution, volume, and reionization history, the simulations show an approximately universal clumping evolution at the 10-20% level when parametrized by the global ionized fraction $x_{\rm HII}$ rather than by redshift. Across all simulations, $C_{\rm rec}$ remains systematically below $C_{\rm HII}$, with the discrepancy increasing toward lower redshift as photoheating suppresses recombinations. In \lumina, the density-only prescription overpredicts the instantaneous recombination rate by factors of 1.29 at $z\approx8$ and 1.84 at $z\approx5$, and the cumulative recombination count by a factor of 1.45 by $z\approx5$. Mapping the recombination budget in the joint overdensity-temperature plane reveals that the dominant recombination ridges closely follow simple analytic thermal equilibrium bands. Finally, we introduce a phase-space recombination integral and define a phase-space clumping factor, $C_{\rm ps}(Δ,T)$, which isolates the intrinsic recombination enhancement associated with ionization structure and thermal state at fixed overdensity and temperature.

AI.tldr: Using Thesan and Lumina simulations, this study shows that clumping factors during reionization evolve nearly universally when parametrized by ionized fraction, with recombination-weighted clumping systematically lower than standard clumping; density-only prescriptions overpredict recombinations, and a new phase-space clumping factor isolates the role of ionization and thermal structure.
AI.motivation: Recombinations during the Epoch of Reionization are intrinsically inhomogeneous, with different IGM regions contributing unevenly depending on density, temperature, ionization state, and spatial patchiness.
AI.method: Combines Thesan-1 (95.5 cMpc, high-res), Thesan-2 (95.5 cMpc, medium-res), and Lumina (500 cMpc) simulations; measures standard (C_HII) and recombination-weighted (C_rec) clumping factors; analyzes recombinations in overdensity-temperature plane; introduces phase-space recombination integral and phase-space clumping factor C_ps(Δ,T).
AI.result: Universal clumping evolution at ~10-20% level when parametrized by x_HII; C_rec < C_HII with increasing discrepancy toward lower z; density-only prescription overpredicts instantaneous recombination rate by factors of 1.29 (z≈8) and 1.84 (z≈5), and cumulative count by 1.45 (z≈5); recombination ridges follow analytic thermal equilibrium bands.
AI.conclusion: Recombinations during reionization are inhomogeneous; clumping factors show ~universal evolution when parametrized by x_HII; C_rec < C_HII; density-only prescriptions overpredict recombination rates; dominant recombination ridges follow analytic thermal equilibrium bands; the phase-space clumping factor C_ps isolates intrinsic recombination enhancement.

title: Short-Duration Gamma-ray Burst and Afterglow Rates in the Rubin and Roman Era
summary: Short-duration gamma-ray burst (sGRB) afterglows that follow BNS-gravitational wave (GW) events are essential for understanding the tension between the observed sGRB rate and BNS merger rate, heightened by the recent conclusion of aLIGO O4 with no new confirmed BNS detections. Using a probabilistic sGRB world model derived from a source BNS merger population, we simulate afterglow emission with AfterglowPy to investigate detection prospects of afterglows in the new era of optical surveys, and probe their multi-messenger implications. The predicted sGRB/BNS association is strongly dependent on sGRB beaming, which may be constrained by orphan afterglows (OA) - that arise from events with no prompt $γ$-ray detection. We conclude that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) may detect an afterglow sample sufficient in constraining sGRB jetting, with an estimated $0.9^{+0.5}_{-0.3}$ on-axis afterglow and $1.3^{+0.9}_{-0.5}$ OA detections per year; while the deep sensitivity of the Roman Space Telescope appears promising for probing the faint end of afterglow events in targeted follow-up strategies. The detection of afterglows in upcoming LIGO runs is possible but challenging, as we predict less than one LSST or Roman discoverable event per year within the projected aLIGO O5 BNS range across all considered jet models and observing scenarios. We update previous sGRB-BNS rate predictions, finding that continued non-detection of a BNS in O5 would require revisiting key assumptions underlying sGRB-BNS models.

AI.tldr: This paper simulates sGRB afterglows from BNS mergers using AfterglowPy to estimate detection rates for LSST and Roman telescopes, finding ~0.9 on-axis and ~1.3 orphan afterglows per year for LSST, but less than one detectable event per year within aLIGO O5 range, highlighting tensions between sGRB and BNS merger rates.
AI.motivation: To resolve the tension between observed sGRB rates and BNS merger rates, especially given the lack of new confirmed BNS detections in aLIGO O4, and to assess future multi-messenger detection prospects for afterglows.
AI.method: Used a probabilistic sGRB world model from a BNS merger population, simulated afterglow emission with AfterglowPy, and estimated detection rates for LSST and Roman Space Telescope under various beaming and observing scenarios.
AI.result: LSST may detect ~0.9 on-axis afterglows and ~1.3 orphan afterglows per year; Roman is promising for faint afterglow follow-ups; less than one LSST/Roman-detectable event per year within aLIGO O5 range; continued O5 non-detection challenges sGRB-BNS model assumptions.
AI.conclusion: sGRB/BNS association strongly depends on sGRB beaming; orphan afterglow detection by LSST can constrain jetting; updated rate predictions suggest that persistent BNS non-detection in O5 would require revisiting core model assumptions.

title: Reconstructing Galactic Gravitational Potentials from Stellar Kinematics with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: The gravitational potential of a galaxy encodes its mass distribution, formation history, and dark matter halo structure. Accurate potential models are therefore critical for interpreting stellar kinematics, orbital dynamics, and the influence of satellite systems like the Large Magellanic Cloud. Analytic potential models offer interpretability and efficiency but struggle to capture complex, non-axisymmetric structure and time-dependent perturbations. Neural network-based methods can capture this complexity but offer little interpretability. We introduce a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that combines data-driven learning with embedded physical constraints, available as the open-source package GalactoPINNS. Trained on acceleration measurements, the framework captures complex, small-scale features while preserving global physical consistency. We test on systems of increasing complexity, from controlled analytic halos to cosmological simulations of Milky Way-like galaxies, achieving sub-percent acceleration errors with orbit reconstruction that consistently outperforms analytic baselines. Additionally, we implement a Bayesian neural network to provide spatially calibrated uncertainty estimates, and a time-dependent extension to capture smooth temporal evolution. By treating an analytic model as a structured prior and learning corrections on top of it, the method retains physical interpretability while gaining the flexibility to represent realistic galactic potentials, making it well suited for Milky Way modeling and dynamical inference in the era of current and upcoming large-scale surveys.

AI.tldr: GalactoPINNS is a physics-informed neural network framework that learns galactic gravitational potentials from acceleration data, combining analytic model interpretability with neural network flexibility, achieving sub-percent acceleration errors and superior orbit reconstruction across systems from analytic halos to cosmological Milky Way simulations.
AI.motivation: Accurate gravitational potential models are critical for interpreting stellar kinematics, orbital dynamics, and satellite system influences, but analytic models struggle with complex non-axisymmetric structure and time-dependent perturbations, while neural networks lack interpretability. A method combining both is needed.
AI.method: A physics-informed neural network (PINN) trained on acceleration measurements, using an analytic model as a structured prior with learned corrections. Includes a Bayesian neural network for spatially calibrated uncertainty estimates and a time-dependent extension for smooth temporal evolution. Implemented as open-source package GalactoPINNS.
AI.result: Achieves sub-percent acceleration errors with orbit reconstruction consistently outperforming analytic baselines, tested on systems from controlled analytic halos to cosmological Milky Way-like galaxy simulations.
AI.conclusion: The method retains physical interpretability while gaining flexibility to represent realistic galactic potentials, making it well suited for Milky Way modeling and dynamical inference in the era of current and upcoming large-scale surveys.

title: SN 2024dy: Dust formation in a long-lived Type IIn supernova and constraints on the dust mass
comment: Accepted version for publication in the ApJ
summary: Type~IIn supernovae (SNe) are a subclass of core-collapse SNe powered by interaction between the ejecta and the dense circumstellar material. Among them, long-lived Type~IIn events are characterized by luminous, long-duration light curves with high radiative energy. Several cases of long-lived type IIn SNe exhibit substantial dust emission at late times. However, well-observed examples remain limited, and the details of their dust formation mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we present photometric and spectroscopic observations of the Type~IIn SN~2024dy in ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared (NIR) wavelength for $500$ days. SN~2024dy reached a peak magnitude of $M_r=-19.2$~mag with a total radiation energy of $1.9\times10^{50}$~erg. A NIR excess emerged at late phases, and the spectral energy distribution modeling indicates the presence of carbon dust with temperatures of $1300$-$1800$~K and masses of about $10^{-5}\ M_\odot$. The spectra features were typical of long-lived Type~IIn SNe. The late time H$α$ profile exhibits a strong suppression of the red wing, providing evidence for newly formed dust. Our results suggest that the derived dust mass above may be underestimated due to optical depth effects. SN~2024dy provides an important observational case for understanding dust formation in Type~IIn SNe.

AI.tldr: SN~2024dy is a Type~IIn supernova observed for 500 days across UV/optical/NIR. It peaked at M_r=-19.2 mag with 1.9e50 erg radiated energy. Late-time NIR excess reveals carbon dust (1300-1800 K, ~1e-5 M_sun). Asymmetric Hα line profiles confirm new dust formation, possibly with underestimated mass due to optical depth.
AI.motivation: Type~IIn SNe are rare and their dust formation mechanisms are poorly understood due to limited well-observed examples. This study aims to characterize dust production in SN~2024dy to improve understanding of dust formation in interacting supernovae.
AI.method: Photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of SN~2024dy across UV, optical, and NIR wavelengths for ~500 days. Spectral energy distribution modeling to constrain dust temperature and mass. Analysis of Hα line profiles to infer dust formation.
AI.result: Peak M_r = -19.2 mag, radiated energy = 1.9e50 erg. Late-phase NIR excess indicates carbon dust at 1300-1800 K with mass ~10^{-5} M_sun. Red-wing suppression in Hα confirms new dust formation. Dust mass likely underestimated due to optical depth.
AI.conclusion: SN~2024dy provides an important observational case study for dust formation in Type~IIn SNe, supporting the picture that these events can produce significant amounts of carbon dust at late times.

title: The Contribution of Disrupted Dense Star Clusters to Gaia's Compact Object Binaries
summary: We present the first model of the Milky Way's detectable compact object--luminous star binary population from disrupted dense star clusters. We bridge large-scale cosmological star cluster formation with high-resolution dynamical evolution of compact object binaries by mapping the predicted star clusters from the EMP-Pathfinder simulations to $N$-body Cluster Monte Carlo models. We predict that approximately $3\times10^5$ white dwarfs (WDs), $1.5\times10^5$ black holes (BHs), and $1\times10^3$ neutron stars (NSs) in binaries with luminous companions are released to the Galaxy from now-disrupted dense star clusters throughout the history of the Milky Way. Synthetic observations modeled with the gaiamock pipeline reveal that the modeled Gaia DR3 yields are sparse ($\approx 2$ WDs, 0 NS, 0 BHs at 90% credibility), with the majority lying beyond the detection horizon. Gaia DR4 is expected to increase the observational yield of these systems only marginally, as the benefits of an expanded search volume are largely offset by the diminished astrometric and photometric precision of more distant sources ($\approx 14$ WDs, 0 NS, 0 BHs). While the underlying BH binary population is similar to that of WDs, they are detected far less frequently; they tend to pair with lower-mass, dimmer companions and have less temporal coverage of their long orbital periods. For NSs, we suggest that the observed over-representation of metal-poor, halo systems is inconsistent with an origin in disrupted dense star clusters. Instead, the observed Gaia NS population could reflect the accretion history of metal-poor, dwarf galaxies into the Milky Way, isolated binary star evolution, or supernova physics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first model of compact object–luminous star binaries (WDs, BHs, NSs) originating from disrupted dense star clusters in the Milky Way, using EMP-Pathfinder simulations and N-body models. It predicts large populations but finds that Gaia DR3 and DR4 will detect very few, with BHs and NSs remaining mostly invisible. The observed metal-poor NS halo population is inconsistent with a disrupted cluster origin and may instead trace dwarf galaxy accretion or binary evolution.
AI.motivation: To model the population of compact object–luminous star binaries released from disrupted dense star clusters in the Milky Way, and to assess their detectability with Gaia, given the current lack of such a model bridging cosmological cluster formation and binary dynamics.
AI.method: Maps star clusters from EMP-Pathfinder cosmological simulations to N-body Cluster Monte Carlo models; uses the gaiamock pipeline for synthetic Gaia observations and statistical yield estimates.
AI.result: Predicts ~3×10^5 WD, ~1.5×10^5 BH, ~1×10^3 NS binaries with luminous companions. Gaia DR3 yields ~2 WDs, 0 NS, 0 BHs; Gaia DR4 yields ~14 WDs, 0 NS, 0 BHs at 90% credibility. BH binaries are similar in number to WDs but detected far less due to dimmer companions and longer orbital periods. Observed metal-poor NS halo population is inconsistent with disrupted cluster origin.
AI.conclusion: Most compact object binaries from disrupted clusters are undetectable by Gaia. BH and NS populations are challenging to detect, while the observed NS halo population likely originates from dwarf galaxy accretion, isolated binary evolution, or supernova physics, not from disrupted dense clusters.

title: A Log-Uniform Initial Magnetic Field Distribution Explains Pulsar and Magnetar Populations through Magnetic Inclination Alignment
summary: The origin of the gap in the observed magnetic field distribution between pulsars and magnetars raises a challenge to understanding these populations within a unified framework. We analytically show that the gap can be naturally explained by the alignment of the magnetic inclination angle between the magnetic and spin axes. Based on coupled evolution of spin-down and magnetic inclination angle in the plasma-filled magnetosphere, the alignment timescale follows $τ_α\propto B^{-2}$. Thus, strongly magnetized neutron stars including high-$B$ pulsars and magnetars align more rapidly than pulsars with $10^{12}\,\mathrm{G}$, reducing their beaming fraction and thereby suppressing their observed numbers. However, magnetars are primarily identified through X-ray activity and are therefore relatively less affected by beaming. Taking into account both beaming fraction and luminosity corrections, we reconstruct the initial magnetic field distribution from the observed distribution. We show that pulsars and magnetars do not dictate intrinsically distinct initial distributions, but can instead be understood within a single continuous initial magnetic field distribution, such as a log-uniform distribution.

AI.tldr: The gap in observed magnetic field distribution between pulsars and magnetars can be explained by the alignment of magnetic inclination angle, where strongly magnetized neutron stars align more rapidly due to τ_α ∝ B^{-2}, reducing their beaming fraction. After correcting for beaming and luminosity, pulsars and magnetars follow a single continuous initial magnetic field distribution (e.g., log-uniform), not distinct populations.
AI.motivation: To resolve the apparent gap in the observed magnetic field distribution between pulsars and magnetars, and to determine whether these two populations originate from distinct physical mechanisms or can be unified under a single formation channel.
AI.method: Analytical modeling of coupled evolution of spin-down and magnetic inclination angle in a plasma-filled magnetosphere, with alignment timescale scaling as τ_α ∝ B^{-2}. Reconstruction of the initial magnetic field distribution from observed data by correcting for beaming fraction and luminosity effects.
AI.result: Strongly magnetized neutron stars (high-B pulsars and magnetars) align more rapidly than ordinary pulsars, reducing their beaming fraction and suppressing observed numbers. After corrections, pulsars and magnetars share a single continuous initial magnetic field distribution (e.g., log-uniform), not intrinsically distinct distributions.
AI.conclusion: Pulsars and magnetars can be understood within a unified framework with a single continuous initial magnetic field distribution; the observed gap is an observational bias due to rapid alignment reducing the beaming fraction of highly magnetized neutron stars.

title: PMO Polaris CO survey. I. A 100 deg$^2$ view of the Polaris Flare
summary: Large-area CO surveys are essential for studying molecular cloud dynamics and evolution; however, most have focused on the Galactic plane, leaving high-latitude clouds less explored. We present the PMO Polaris CO Survey (PPCOS), which maps a 100~deg$^2$ region of the Polaris Flare in the $J=1-0$ transitions of $^{12}$CO, $^{13}$CO, and C$^{18}$O using the Delingha 13.7~m telescope. As the first large-area CO survey at high Galactic latitude ($|b| > 20^{\circ}$) with sub-arcminute resolution, PPCOS achieves sensitivities of $\sim$0.46~K for $^{12}$CO and $\sim$0.23~K for $^{13}$CO and C$^{18}$O at a spectral resolution of 0.16~km~s$^{-1}$ and an angular resolution of 50\arcsec. The $^{12}$CO emission reveals seven distinct complexes, where only $\sim$10\% of pixels display multiple velocity components, alongside a global velocity gradient of 0.18~km~s$^{-1}$~pc$^{-1}$. Typical line widths are $1.2 \pm 0.6$~\mbox{km~s$^{-1}$} for $^{12}$CO, while $^{13}$CO components are systematically narrower ($\lesssim 0.7\,ΔV_{\rm ^{12}CO}$). The $^{12}$CO/$^{13}$CO intensity ratios (5--25) indicate widespread $^{12}$CO optical thickness, resembling conditions found in giant molecular clouds (GMCs). Globally, the CO emission divides into two groups: a major group aligned with the velocity gradient and a secondary group elongated perpendicular to it, possibly regulated by large-scale coherent dynamics. We propose a three-layer hierarchy: a dynamically assembling and dispersing periphery traced by $^{12}$CO, a more stable intermediate kernel traced by $^{13}$CO, and gravitationally bound compact cores traced by C$^{18}$O. No young stellar objects are firmly associated with the molecular gas. PPCOS provides an ideal laboratory for studying turbulence, hierarchical structure, and early cloud evolution in a nearby, relatively simple molecular cloud.

AI.tldr: PPCOS mapped a 100 deg² region of the Polaris Flare in ¹²CO, ¹³CO, and C¹⁸O using the Delingha 13.7m telescope, achieving sub-arcminute resolution at high Galactic latitude. It reveals seven complexes, simple kinematics (only ~10% multi-component), a global velocity gradient of 0.18 km/s/pc, and a three-layer hierarchy (¹²CO periphery, ¹³CO intermediate, C¹⁸O cores) with no associated YSOs, serving as a laboratory for early molecular cloud evolution.
AI.motivation: Large-area CO surveys have focused on the Galactic plane, leaving high-latitude clouds (|b|>20°) underexplored despite their importance for studying molecular cloud dynamics and evolution in simpler environments.
AI.method: Mapping a 100 deg² region of the Polaris Flare in ¹²CO, ¹³CO, and C¹⁸O (J=1-0) with the Delingha 13.7m telescope, achieving sensitivities of ~0.46 K (¹²CO) and ~0.23 K (¹³CO, C¹⁸O) at 0.16 km/s spectral resolution and 50″ angular resolution.
AI.result: Seven distinct complexes identified; only ~10% of pixels show multiple velocity components; global velocity gradient of 0.18 km/s/pc; typical ¹²CO line widths 1.2±0.6 km/s; ¹³CO narrower (≤0.7×ΔV_¹²CO); ¹²CO/¹³CO intensity ratios 5-25 indicating widespread ¹²CO optical thickness; CO emission divides into two groups (major aligned with velocity gradient, secondary perpendicular); three-layer hierarchy proposed; no firmly associated YSOs.
AI.conclusion: PPCOS provides an ideal laboratory for studying turbulence, hierarchical structure, and early cloud evolution in a nearby, relatively simple molecular cloud at high Galactic latitude.

title: Discovery of a 24-millisecond pulsar in a very long orbit with the Murchison Widefield Array
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: We report the discovery of PSR J0125$-$5854, a pulsar with a spin period of 24 ms and a dispersion measure of 11.66 pc cm$^-3$ in the ongoing Southern-sky MWA Rapid Two-metre (SMART) survey with the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). The pulsar is located at a high Galactic latitude of $-57^{\circ}$, and at a distance of 0.5$\text{-}$1 kpc per the Galactic electron density models. Follow-up observations with the MWA and MeerKAT telescopes have revealed that this pulsar is in a binary system with an orbital period of more than 290 days, and a steep spectrum (flux density, $ S \propto ν^α $, where $ν$ is frequency and $ α= -2.2 \pm 0.3 $). Analysis of current observational data hints at a potential binary configuration with an orbital period of $833.60 \pm 0.04$ days, a projected semi-major axis of $241.36 \pm 0.05$ light-seconds, and a minimum companion mass $0.4152 \pm 0.0001$ M$_\odot$, with a low eccentricity orbit of $0.0052 \pm 0.0006$. We discuss the potential formation channels for this system, and conjecture that the companion is likely a Helium white dwarf. Further observations are required in order to better constrain the orbital and spin parameters. We discuss the implications of this discovery, which emerged after processing a small fraction of survey data, on the prospects of finding more millisecond pulsars with the SMART survey, and with future surveys planned with the low-frequency SKA-Low.

AI.tldr: Discovery of PSR J0125−5854, a 24 ms millisecond pulsar in a long-period binary (P_orb ~833 days) with a steep spectrum, low eccentricity, and a likely helium white dwarf companion, found in the SMART survey using MWA and followed up with MeerKAT.
AI.motivation: To detect new millisecond pulsars via the low-frequency SMART survey using the MWA, and to understand the formation channels of binary pulsar systems, particularly those with probable He white dwarf companions at high Galactic latitude.
AI.method: Discovery and timing analysis using the MWA (SMART survey) and follow-up with MeerKAT; measurement of spin period, dispersion measure, spectral index, and derivation of orbital parameters (period, semi-major axis, eccentricity, minimum companion mass) via pulsar timing.
AI.result: Found a 24 ms pulsar at high Galactic latitude (−57°), DM=11.66 pc cm⁻³, distance 0.5–1 kpc; binary with P_orb=833.60±0.04 d, projected semi-major axis=241.36±0.05 lt-s, eccentricity=0.0052±0.0006, min companion mass=0.4152±0.0001 M⊙; steep spectral index α=−2.2±0.3.
AI.conclusion: The companion is likely a Helium white dwarf; further observations needed to refine parameters; the discovery demonstrates the potential of the SMART survey and future SKA-Low surveys for finding more millisecond pulsars.

title: Disentangling the Distant Stellar Halo Using K-Giants in the DESI Year 3 Data
comment: 39 pages, 25 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present a sample of 88,959 K-giants from DESI Milky Way Survey Year 3 data, which we use to characterize the chemo-dynamical properties of the stellar halo at Galactocentric distances of 12 to ~100 kpc. Using HDBSCAN, we identify five prominent stellar halo substructures: Aleph, the Sagittarius stream, Gaia Sausage-Enceladus (GSE), Cetus-Palca and the Orphan-Chenab stream. We present the properties of each of these structures as they appear in our catalog, and examine how uncertainties on distance affect the characterization of substructure with this approach. We also examine regions associated with previously reported overdensities (such as the Virgo Overdensities and the Sagittarius spur) that we do not recover with HDBSCAN. The size and distance range of our catalog allows us to explore in detail the residual stellar halo, comprising stars that we do not associate with any substructure. We find that samples of ~2000 outer halo stars with both highly prograde and highly retrograde angular momenta have similar metallicity distribution functions (MDFs), which do not resemble the MDFs of either GSE or Sagittarius. Both the prograde and retrograde residual halo MDFs are bimodal, with a metal-poor peak at [Fe/H] ~ -2 and a metal-rich peak at [Fe/H] ~ -1.3 (prograde) or -1.5 (retrograde). The MDF for lower angular momentum residual halo K-giants does not show clear evidence for a metal-poor peak, and broadly resembles the MDF of GSE, even at much lower binding energies than GSE itself. We discuss possible interpretations of these findings for GSE accretion scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes 88,959 K-giants from DESI Milky Way Survey Year 3 data to characterize stellar halo chemo-dynamical properties at 12–100 kpc. Using HDBSCAN, it identifies five substructures (Aleph, Sagittarius stream, GSE, Cetus-Palca, Orphan-Chenab) and examines the residual halo's metallicity distribution functions, finding bimodal MDFs for high angular momentum stars and GSE-like MDFs for low angular momentum stars.
AI.motivation: To characterize the chemo-dynamical properties of the Milky Way's stellar halo at large Galactocentric distances (12–100 kpc) using a large sample of K-giants, and to understand the nature of the residual halo after accounting for known substructures.
AI.method: Analysis of 88,959 K-giants from DESI Milky Way Survey Year 3 data; HDBSCAN clustering for substructure identification; examination of metallicity distribution functions (MDFs) for different angular momentum bins of the residual halo.
AI.result: Five substructures identified (Aleph, Sagittarius, GSE, Cetus-Palca, Orphan-Chenab). Residual halo shows: (1) highly prograde and retrograde samples (~2000 stars) have similar bimodal MDFs (metal-poor peak at [Fe/H]~-2, metal-rich peak at -1.3 or -1.5), distinct from GSE/Sagittarius; (2) low angular momentum residual halo MDF resembles GSE's MDF even at much lower binding energies.
AI.conclusion: The residual stellar halo exhibits distinct chemo-dynamical populations: high angular momentum stars (both prograde and retrograde) share a bimodal MDF unlike known substructures, while low angular momentum stars resemble GSE, suggesting complex GSE accretion scenarios and multiple origins for the outer halo.

title: \texttt{TransFit-MAG}: Self-Consistent Modeling of Magnetar-Powered Transients from Shock Breakout to Spin-Down Heating
summary: Magnetar engines are widely invoked to power luminous optical transients, but their early emission depends on the coupled evolution of engine injection, shock heating, adiabatic cooling, and radiative diffusion. We present \texttt{TransFit-MAG}, a time-dependent radiative-diffusion framework for magnetar-powered transients. The model couples the \texttt{TransFit} diffusion solver to the dynamics of a magnetar-inflated pulsar wind nebula (PWN) and its forward shock propagating through homologously expanding ejecta, calculating the internal radiation-energy distribution, photospheric evolution, shock-heating location, and emergent luminosity self-consistently. For different parameter values, the model naturally produces well-separated double peaks, partially merged peaks, or single broad peaks. These results suggest that early bumps and broad single peaks in engine-powered transients may be understood within a unified engine--shock--diffusion framework, in which the observed diversity reflects the coupled evolution of central-engine power, shock propagation, and radiative transport through expanding ejecta. As an illustrative application, we fit the multiband optical light curves of the double-peaked SLSN-I LSQ14bdq.

AI.tldr: The paper presents \texttt{TransFit-MAG}, a time-dependent radiative-diffusion framework for magnetar-powered transients that self-consistently couples engine injection, shock heating, adiabatic cooling, and radiative diffusion. It unifies diverse observed light-curve morphologies (double peaks, merged peaks, single broad peaks) within a single physical model and demonstrates application to the double-peaked SLSN-I LSQ14bdq.
AI.motivation: Magnetar engines are widely invoked to power luminous optical transients, but their early emission depends on the coupled evolution of engine injection, shock heating, adiabatic cooling, and radiative diffusion — a complex interplay not captured by existing models.
AI.method: The authors present \texttt{TransFit-MAG}, a time-dependent radiative-diffusion framework that couples the \texttt{TransFit} diffusion solver to the dynamics of a magnetar-inflated pulsar wind nebula (PWN) and its forward shock propagating through homologously expanding ejecta, calculating internal radiation-energy distribution, photospheric evolution, shock-heating location, and emergent luminosity self-consistently.
AI.result: For different parameter values, the model naturally produces well-separated double peaks, partially merged peaks, or single broad peaks. This suggests that early bumps and broad single peaks in engine-powered transients can be understood within a unified engine–shock–diffusion framework where observed diversity reflects coupled evolution of central-engine power, shock propagation, and radiative transport.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies diverse light-curve morphologies of magnetar-powered transients. As an illustrative application, the model successfully fits the multiband optical light curves of the double-peaked SLSN-I LSQ14bdq.

title: Searching for a superdisk in radio galaxy J0116-473
summary: Superdisks have emerged as an active area of research in recent years, and J0116-473 represents a promising target for studying this extended structure. Our primary objective was to search for HI absorption associated with the suspected superdisk. However, no such absorption feature was detected, suggesting a low, or absence of neutral hydrogen content in the superdisk. In addition, we examined a compact point source located near the galaxy's core and the presumed plane of the superdisk, enabling us to search for HI absorption against this background continuum. We also present a detailed multi-band morphological analysis of the galaxy using Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) observations in Bands 3, 4, and 5. A spectral analysis of both the galaxy and the nearby point source was carried out using data from these three frequency bands. A systematic steepening of the spectral index is observed from the core toward the lobes, as expected for aging synchrotron-emitting plasma. We also found that the northern inner lobe exhibits a significantly steeper spectrum than its southern counterpart, possibly reflecting environmental effects associated with the proposed superdisk. Since superdisks are expected to contain hot, ionized gas, we additionally examined archival X-ray observations from the XMM-Newton telescope. Although diffuse X-ray emission associated with the radio lobes is visible, no significant emission is detected from the region corresponding to the suspected superdisk.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-wavelength study of galaxy J0116-473 to search for HI absorption and X-ray emission from a suspected superdisk. No HI absorption was detected, indicating low neutral hydrogen content. Spectral analysis reveals steepening from core to lobes, with the northern inner lobe steeper than the southern one, possibly due to environmental effects from the superdisk. X-ray observations show no significant emission from the superdisk region.
AI.motivation: To search for HI absorption associated with a suspected superdisk in J0116-473, and to characterize the morphology and spectral properties of the galaxy and its surrounding structures.
AI.method: GMRT multi-band (Bands 3, 4, 5) radio observations for HI absorption search, spectral index mapping, and morphological analysis, supplemented by archival XMM-Newton X-ray observations.
AI.result: No HI absorption detected from the superdisk. Spectral index steepens systematically from core to lobes; the northern inner lobe has a significantly steeper spectrum than the southern one. No significant X-ray emission from the superdisk region, though diffuse X-ray emission associated with radio lobes is visible.
AI.conclusion: The suspected superdisk in J0116-473 likely contains little to no neutral hydrogen and lacks detectable X-ray emission, but may influence the spectral properties of the inner lobes through environmental interactions.

title: Pinning Down the Geometry of the Type Ic Broad-Line Supernova 2026gzf
summary: Type Ic broad-line supernovae (SNe Ic-BL) are often associated with energetic explosions that display a prompt outburst of high-energy emission. Since their progenitor lost the H and He envelopes before the explosion exposing the C/O core, their explosion dynamics and geometry can be seen in an unobscured and undistorted way. We present imaging polarimetry and spectropolarimetry of the Type Ic-BL SN 2026gzf obtained 4.6 and 16.5 days after the X-ray shock breakout, which was recorded by the Einstein Probe satellite as EP260321a, showing it to be one of the softest and intrinsically dimmest extragalactic fast X-ray transients. The persistent low continuum polarization indicates that the outer layer of SN 2026gzf is mostly spherical, suggesting the explosion did not significantly disrupt the progenitor envelope. At day 16.5, the calcium near-infrared triplet displays a peak polarization above 1.5%. The geometry of the associated line opacity is also compatible with an axisymmetric configuration. The spatial distribution of such oxygen-burning ashes thus indicates the presence of a symmetry axis of the excitation structure within the nearly spherical ejecta. The Ca II triplet profile is dominated by a primary component spanning ~25,000--40,000 km/s, alongside a distinct secondary component extending above 28,000 km/s whose polarization implies a non-axisymmetric, complex excitation geometry toward the outer ejecta By implementing a three-dimensional Monte-Carlo calculation, we infer that a viewing angle of ~40 degree from the symmetry axis of the excitation structure could plausibly reproduce the observed spectral and polarization profiles of the Ca II triplet.

AI.tldr: SN 2026gzf (EP260321a) is a Type Ic-BL supernova with a mostly spherical outer ejecta, but axisymmetric Ca II triplet emission at ~40° viewing angle, showing complex excitation geometry in the oxygen-burning ashes.
AI.motivation: To understand the explosion dynamics and geometry of Type Ic-BL supernovae through polarimetric observations, leveraging the unobscured view of their stripped progenitor envelopes.
AI.method: Imaging polarimetry and spectropolarimetry at 4.6 and 16.5 days post X-ray shock breakout, combined with 3D Monte-Carlo radiative transfer calculations to infer viewing angle and excitation geometry.
AI.result: Low continuum polarization implies a spherical outer layer; Ca II near-infrared triplet shows >1.5% peak polarization at day 16.5, with primary (25,000-40,000 km/s) and secondary (>28,000 km/s) velocity components. A ~40° viewing angle from the symmetry axis reproduces observations.
AI.conclusion: The explosion did not significantly disrupt the progenitor envelope; the oxygen-burning ashes (traced by Ca II) reveal an axisymmetric excitation structure with a symmetry axis embedded within nearly spherical ejecta, and the outer ejecta exhibits non-axisymmetric, complex geometry.

title: A comparative study of O, Ne, Cl, and Ar in Hii regions and PNe of the Galactic disk: Temporal evolution of radial gradients?
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Additional four long tables in the appendix (16 pages). Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: (Abridged) We compare the radial abundance gradients of O, Ne, Cl, and Ar using a sample of 42 HII regions and 176 planetary nebulae (PNe) from the DESIRED catalogue in the Galactic disk, comprising the highest-quality observations currently available and presenting the first gradient analysis for this dataset. For all objects, two sets of chemical abundances were compiled: one derived from collisionally excited lines (CELs) and another incorporating the temperature fluctuation parameter (t^2). Oxygen abundances were corrected for dust depletion, and HII region results were compared with Cepheid stars, which trace the present-day interstellar medium. PNe distances were compiled from recent literature, excluding bulge or halo objects to ensure a disk-only sample. All gradients are statistically significant (p < 0.05), except for Cl and Ar in HII regions. The O/H gradients from HII regions and Cepheids are consistent when t^2 is included, underscoring the importance of accounting for temperature inhomogeneities in nebular analyses. The O and Ne gradients traced by older objects are flatter than the present-day gradient by -0.028 +- 0.008 dex kpc-1 on average from both RLs and CELs. This could indicate a temporal steepening of the Galactic abundance gradient; however, this behavior is not reproduced by chemical evolution models, suggesting additional physical processes are at play. The most plausible explanation is that our PNe sample has been strongly affected by radial migration. Under this interpretation, the PNe gradient cannot reliably trace past abundance gradients, but provides a valuable constraint on radial stellar migration, offering important input for chemo-dynamical models of the Galactic disk and for hydrodynamical simulations.

AI.tldr: This study compares radial abundance gradients (O, Ne, Cl, Ar) between 42 HII regions and 176 planetary nebulae in the Galactic disk using the DESIRED catalogue. When accounting for temperature fluctuations (t²), O/H gradients from HII regions match those from Cepheids. Older objects (PNe) show flatter gradients than present-day ones, possibly due to radial stellar migration rather than genuine temporal steepening, as chemical evolution models do not reproduce this flattening.
AI.motivation: To compare present-day (HII regions, Cepheids) and older (planetary nebulae) abundance gradients in the Galactic disk using the highest-quality DESIRED dataset, and to understand whether gradient differences reflect temporal evolution of the Galaxy or are influenced by processes like radial migration.
AI.method: A sample of 42 HII regions and 176 PNe from the DESIRED catalogue was analyzed. Abundances were derived using two methods: collisionally excited lines (CELs) and incorporating the temperature fluctuation parameter (t²). Oxygen abundances were dust-depletion corrected. HII region gradients were compared with Cepheid data. PNe distances came from recent literature; bulge/halo objects were excluded.
AI.result: All gradients are statistically significant (p<0.05) except Cl and Ar in HII regions. O/H gradients from HII regions and Cepheids are consistent when t² is included. O and Ne gradients from older objects are flatter than present-day by -0.028±0.008 dex kpc⁻¹. Chemical evolution models do not reproduce this flattening.
AI.conclusion: The flatter gradients in PNe likely reflect radial stellar migration rather than genuine temporal steepening. Thus, PNe gradients are not reliable tracers of past abundance gradients but instead provide constraints on radial migration, informing chemo-dynamical models and hydrodynamical simulations of the Galactic disk.

title: A thick-shell formalism for pulsar wind nebulae based on energy conservation
summary: One of the most powerful approaches to model the structural and spectral evolution of wind bubbles, and pulsar wind nebulae in particular, is based on the one-zone thin-shell formalism. By solving a set of simple equations, one can relate the spectral properties of these systems to the physical properties of the pulsar and supernova remnant. Due to its predictive power, this approach has been widely used both to fit existing objects and in population synthesis. However, there are inconsistencies when applied to the Crab nebula that have never been fully accounted for, casting doubts on its reliability. We introduce a new and more flexible formalism based on energy conservation that reconciles the observed structural and spectral properties of the Crab nebula, solving the inconsistencies, and provides a more realistic description of wind-bubble evolution. The equations of the formalism are presented and discussed, together with simplified solutions and more complex ones including radiation losses. Implications for the modeling of wind bubbles and pulsar wind nebulae are illustrated. We also introduce a new high-order upwind-implicit scheme for particle-spectrum evolution that ensures high accuracy in energy conservation, and an algebraic-vectorizable approach for synchrotron self-Compton emission in the full Klein-Nishina regime that avoids costly interpolations and integrations. We reproduce the Crab nebula structural properties and spectrum, accounting for the difference in convergence age between the optical filaments and the radio bubble, thereby removing the inconsistencies. The spectral accuracy of this approach is comparable to that of the standard one, but it is superior in reproducing structural properties and accounting for geometrical effects such as a thick layer of mixed material and the lack of efficient coupling between the wind bubble and the surrounding medium.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new energy-conservation-based formalism for modeling wind bubbles and pulsar wind nebulae, resolving inconsistencies in the thin-shell formalism when applied to the Crab nebula, and includes improved numerical schemes for particle spectrum and synchrotron self-Compton emission.
AI.motivation: The standard one-zone thin-shell formalism, despite being widely used, produces inconsistencies when applied to the Crab nebula, casting doubt on its reliability for modeling wind bubbles and pulsar wind nebulae.
AI.method: A new energy-conservation-based formalism is introduced, along with a high-order upwind-implicit scheme for particle-spectrum evolution and an algebraic-vectorizable approach for synchrotron self-Compton emission in the full Klein-Nishina regime.
AI.result: The new formalism successfully reproduces the Crab nebula's structural properties and spectrum, accounting for the difference in convergence age between optical filaments and the radio bubble, thereby removing previous inconsistencies.
AI.conclusion: The new approach is comparable in spectral accuracy to the standard one but superior in reproducing structural properties and accounting for geometrical effects such as thick mixed-material layers and inefficient coupling between the wind bubble and surrounding medium.

title: IllustrisTNG50 angular momentum maps: tracing the morpho-kinematic evolution of galaxies
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures, submitted to a&a, comments are welcome, modified abstract to fit Arxiv requirements
summary: Following the first observational study of the two-dimensional spatial distribution of stellar specific angular momentum (sAM) in late-type galaxies, we quantify the morpho-kinematic diversity of galaxy simulations using the newly proposed j-types classification. We analyse the stellar sAM surface density (sAMSD) of $\sim$8000 TNG50 stellar discs spanning $0 \leq z \leq 3.5$ and $9.5 \leq \log(M_\star/\mathrm{M}_\odot) \leq 11.2$, selected from the TNG50 MW/M31 parent sample. We characterize their j-substructures using four morpho-kinematic metrics derived from comparisons with the Freeman sAMSD distribution and the Fourier decomposition of the galaxies in the sAMSD space. A Gaussian mixture model with four fully covariant components assigns each galaxy a probability of belonging to one of four j-types. We find that TNG50 discs exhibit a morpho-kinematic diversity consistent with observations, redistributing stellar angular momentum through four dominant j-substructures that evolve with redshift as follows: j-irregulars ($\bar{z}=0.91$), j-spirals ($\bar{z}=0.76$), j-rings ($\bar{z}=0.62$), and j-bars ($\bar{z}=0.39$). The gas fraction and stellar rotational support ($V/σ$) drive this evolution: gas-rich galaxies preferentially host j-irregulars and j-spirals, whereas gas-poor systems favour j-rings and j-bars. At fixed gas fraction, higher $V/σ$ favours j-spirals and j-rings, respectively. We conclude that there is a canonical pathway for the redistribution of angular momentum within galactic discs undergoing secular evolution in TNG50, accessible only through their morpho-kinematic description. The sAMSD analysis links variations in stellar dynamics to their consequences for mass redistribution, enabling the reconstruction of comprehensive galactic evolutionary histories.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes ~8000 TNG50 simulated stellar discs (z=0–3.5) using a new morpho-kinematic classification (j-types) based on stellar specific angular momentum surface density (sAMSD). Four j-types are identified—j-irregulars, j-spirals, j-rings, j-bars—whose prevalence evolves with redshift, driven by gas fraction and stellar rotational support (V/σ). The study reveals a canonical pathway for angular momentum redistribution linked to secular disc evolution.
AI.motivation: Following the first observational study of 2D stellar specific angular momentum distribution in late-type galaxies, the authors aim to quantify the morpho-kinematic diversity of simulated galaxies using the newly proposed j-types classification, connecting simulations to observations.
AI.method: The authors analyze stellar sAMSD of ~8000 TNG50 stellar discs (z=0–3.5, M⋆=10^9.5–10^11.2 M☉) from the TNG50 MW/M31 parent sample. They characterize j-substructures using four morpho-kinematic metrics derived from comparisons with Freeman sAMSD distribution and Fourier decomposition in sAMSD space. A Gaussian mixture model with four fully covariant components assigns each galaxy a probability of belonging to one of four j-types.
AI.result: TNG50 discs show morpho-kinematic diversity consistent with observations, with four dominant j-substructures that evolve with redshift: j-irregulars (z̄=0.91), j-spirals (z̄=0.76), j-rings (z̄=0.62), and j-bars (z̄=0.39). Gas fraction and V/σ drive this evolution: gas-rich galaxies host j-irregulars/spirals; gas-poor systems favor j-rings/bars. At fixed gas fraction, higher V/σ favors j-spirals and j-rings.
AI.conclusion: There is a canonical pathway for angular momentum redistribution in galactic discs undergoing secular evolution in TNG50, accessible through their morpho-kinematic description. sAMSD analysis links stellar dynamics variations to mass redistribution consequences, enabling reconstruction of comprehensive galactic evolutionary histories.

title: The flash-ionised SN Ibn 2025kzr: H-free CSM formed during a precursor outburst 55 days prior to explosion
summary: Type Ibn supernovae (SNe) are a class of interacting SNe characterised by narrow helium lines in their spectra. We present an extensive observational dataset of the Type Ibn SN 2025kzr at 51 Mpc, including the discovery of a precursor outburst with a peak brightness of M_r~-13.6 mag beginning ~55 days before explosion. Our photometry indicates the SN was discovered within the first day of explosion, showing fast-rising, ultraviolet-bright emission peaking at M_r=-19.26+/-0.09 mag and a peak blackbody temperature of T~29000 K, consistent with shock breakout within a region of dense and confined circumstellar material (CSM). Our high-cadence spectroscopic dataset spanning 1.9-58.5 days post-explosion shows flash-ionised emission features during the first 10 days. In our SALT spectrum at 3.8 days we observe a pronounced blueshift of the He II lines by 460 km/s compared to the He I lines at zero velocity, while a Pickering-decrement analysis reveals a CSM that is fully hydrogen-free. The timing of the disappearance of the flash features combined with the CSM velocity of 1500 km/s imply a mass-loss event ~66 days before explosion, in close agreement with the timing of the precursor observed 55 days before explosion and strongly suggestive of a physical link. We derive a CSM mass of 0.03-1.7 M_sun and a corresponding high mass-loss rate >~10^{-1} M_sun/yr. The precursor timescale and energetics suggest an extreme mass-loss event that might be explained by wave-driven mass loss during the late stages of nuclear burning, in particular the oxygen-burning phase. Overall, we favour a single massive Wolf-Rayet progenitor with M_ZAMS~30-40 M_sun to explain SN 2025kzr, although a binary origin cannot be excluded.

AI.tldr: SN 2025kzr is a Type Ibn supernova at 51 Mpc with a precursor outburst ~55 days before explosion, fast-rising UV-bright emission, flash-ionised spectral features, a hydrogen-free CSM, and a derived CSM mass of 0.03–1.7 M☉. The progenitor is likely a single Wolf-Rayet star of ~30–40 M☉.
AI.motivation: To characterise the early evolution and progenitor system of Type Ibn SN 2025kzr through extensive multi-wavelength photometry and high-cadence spectroscopy, particularly focusing on its precursor outburst and CSM interaction.
AI.method: Observational dataset including photometry (discovery ~first day, fast-rising UV-bright emission), high-cadence spectroscopy (1.9–58.5 days post-explosion), SALT spectrum at 3.8 days for He II line blueshift analysis, Pickering-decrement analysis for hydrogen content, and modelling of CSM mass and mass-loss rate.
AI.result: Precursor outburst at M_r~−13.6 mag ~55 days pre-explosion; SN peak M_r=−19.26±0.09 mag with T~29,000 K; He II lines blueshifted by 460 km/s relative to He I; hydrogen-free CSM; flash features vanish ~66 days after mass-loss event (1500 km/s), matching precursor timing; CSM mass 0.03–1.7 M☉; mass-loss rate >~10⁻¹ M☉/yr.
AI.conclusion: The precursor and CSM properties point to an extreme mass-loss event ~66 days before explosion, likely driven by wave-driven mass loss during late nuclear burning (oxygen-burning phase). A single massive Wolf-Rayet progenitor (M_ZAMS~30–40 M☉) is favoured; a binary origin is possible but less likely.

title: Solitary dwarf galaxy groups as tracers of primordial dark matter halos in the local Universe
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables, submitted to RAA
summary: In $Λ$CDM cosmology, galaxies and clusters form within dark matter halos and merge in the hierarchical assembly paradigm to form massive systems. Using the released optical survey data, we searched for groups composed solely of dwarf galaxies, each with a stellar mass $M_*<10^{9.5}~M_{\odot}$. We identified 14 dwarf galaxy groups with at least 5 dwarf galaxies, all located within a projected radius of 200 kpc and with a line-of-sight velocity of $\pm$300 km~s$^{-1}$. We checked photometric and imaging data and found that these 14 dwarf galaxy groups are solitary, with no neighboring massive galaxies with $M_*>10^{10}~M_{\odot}$ within 500 kpc and within $\pm$1200 km s$^{-1}$. The stellar mass fractions of dwarf galaxy groups with $M_{\rm dyn}>10^{12}~M_{\odot}$ are much lower than predicted by the canonical stellar mass and halo mass relation. These dwarf galaxies are gravitationally bound within halos with a dynamical mass of around $M_{\rm dyn} \sim 10^{12}~M_{\odot}$ and a virial radius of less than 400 kpc. These dwarf galaxy groups, therefore, indicate primordial halos that host only a few newly formed dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using optical survey data, the study identifies 14 isolated dwarf galaxy groups (each with ≥5 dwarf galaxies, M*<10^9.5 M☉) that have no neighboring massive galaxies within 500 kpc. These groups have dynamical masses ~10^12 M☉ and virial radii <400 kpc, with stellar mass fractions much lower than canonical predictions, suggesting they are primordial halos hosting only newly formed dwarf galaxies.
AI.motivation: To search for galaxy groups composed solely of dwarf galaxies in ΛCDM cosmology and investigate whether such primordial halos exist without massive galaxies, testing hierarchical assembly predictions.
AI.method: Optical survey data were used to identify dwarf galaxy groups (M*<10^9.5 M☉, ≥5 members) within a projected radius of 200 kpc and line-of-sight velocity ±300 km/s. Photometric and imaging checks ensured no neighboring massive galaxies (M*>10^10 M☉) within 500 kpc and ±1200 km/s. Dynamical masses and stellar mass fractions were computed.
AI.result: 14 isolated dwarf galaxy groups were found. Their stellar mass fractions are much lower than the canonical stellar-to-halo mass relation for systems with M_dyn>10^12 M☉. The groups are gravitationally bound in halos of ~10^12 M☉ dynamical mass and <400 kpc virial radius.
AI.conclusion: These dwarf galaxy groups represent primordial halos that host only a few newly formed dwarf galaxies, offering insights into early galaxy formation and hierarchical merging processes.

title: 2D magnetohydrodynamic jet simulations: properties of recollimation shocks
comment: 18 pages, 21 figures, 2 tables, submitted in A&A
summary: Recollimation shocks are a frequent outcome in overpressured relativistic jets and are crucial for interpreting stationary features in Active Galactic Nuclei. The precise influence of magnetic fields on jet stability, energy dissipation, and variability remains debated, particularly as different field configurations can significantly alter shock properties and the onset of fluid instabilities. We perform a study of 2D axisymmetric RMHD jets to quantify how the ambient density contrast ($ν$), pressure ratio ($P$), magnetization ($σ$), and magnetic pitch parameter ($α$) govern the formation and strength of the first recollimation shock. We also assess how these parameters create the local geometric conditions favorable for the centrifugal instability (CFI), utilizing linear theory as a diagnostic. We find that the jet's global geometry is affected by the magnetic pressure. The recollimation distance decreases monotonically with increasing magnetization $σ$, as increased magnetic forces immediately limit jet expansion. Remarkably, in the magnetically dominated regime, the ratio of the magnetized recollimation distance ($z_{\rm MHD}$) to its purely hydrodynamic counterpart ($z_{\rm HD}$) converges onto a power-law scaling, $z_{MHD}/z_{HD} \propto (B_0^2/P_{ext})^{-1/3}$, where $B_0$ the initial magnetic field and $P_{ext}$ the external pressure. Jets with high density contrast relative to the ambient medium or high internal pressure further enhance field compression. Furthermore, synthetic synchrotron maps show that a dominant toroidal field yields highly boosted, localized emission knots, whereas a strong poloidal field creates a diffuse profile and shifts the recollimation zone downstream. Regions susceptible to CFI are determined primarily by the local $σ_{\text{tor}}/Γ^2$ profile and streamline curvature created during recollimation.

AI.tldr: This 2D axisymmetric RMHD simulation study investigates how magnetic field parameters (magnetization σ, magnetic pitch α, density contrast ν, pressure ratio P) control recollimation shock formation and centrifugal instability in relativistic jets, finding that magnetic pressure reduces recollimation distance with a specific power-law scaling, and that field topology (toroidal vs. poloidal) strongly influences synchrotron emission morphology and instability-prone regions.
AI.motivation: Recollimation shocks are important for interpreting stationary features in AGN jets, but the role of magnetic fields in jet stability, energy dissipation, and variability is debated. This work aims to quantify how key magnetic and hydrodynamic parameters govern shock formation and instability conditions.
AI.method: 2D axisymmetric RMHD simulations with varying density contrast (ν), pressure ratio (P), magnetization (σ), and magnetic pitch parameter (α); linear theory diagnostics for centrifugal instability (CFI); synthetic synchrotron maps for observational comparison.
AI.result: (1) Recollimation distance decreases monotonically with σ due to magnetic pressure limiting jet expansion. (2) In magnetically dominated regime, z_MHD/z_HD ∝ (B₀²/P_ext)^{-1/3}. (3) High density contrast or internal pressure enhances field compression. (4) Toroidal field produces boosted, localized emission knots; poloidal field yields diffuse profiles and downstream recollimation. (5) CFI susceptibility governed by local σ_tor/Γ² profile and streamline curvature.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic field configuration fundamentally controls recollimation shock properties and instability development in relativistic jets, with implications for interpreting observed AGN jet morphology and variability.

title: Ages of the resolved stellar populations inside the JWST/MIRI bubbles in NGC 628
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 18 pages, 16 figures and 2 tables
summary: JWST images in the MIRI filters are characterized by prominent interstellar bubbles, most of which are expected to be created by mechanical energy injected into the interstellar medium by dying massive stars. In this work, we use resolved stellar populations (RSPs) in JWST/NIRCam images of NGC 628 from the JWST-FEAST dataset to determine the demography of stellar populations within these bubbles by comparing them with PARSEC+COLIBRI isochrones using a Bayesian framework. Our analysis reveals the presence of multiple stellar populations younger than 100 Myr within the bubbles, suggesting secondary star formation following the first generation of stars that formed the bubble. We find a clear preference for the most recently formed stars to lie closer to the bubble shell. In contrast, relatively older stars are distributed throughout the bubble interior, consistent with a scenario in which stars formed in dense shells are left behind as the shell expands. We also examine PHANGS-HST cluster candidates within large bubbles and find no convincing progenitor clusters responsible for the initial trigger, indicating that low-mass clusters or OB associations may be sufficient to drive the initial expansion. However, the cluster may dissolve as it co-evolves with the bubble, producing the dispersed stellar distributions observed in larger bubbles. We establish a fundamental plane relation for stellar feedback-driven bubbles that involves the stellar population mass, age, bubble size, gas density, and feedback efficiency, highlighting the ability of JWST/NIRCam CMDs to characterize stellar populations driving interstellar bubble expansion in nearby galaxies

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRCam resolved stellar populations in NGC 628, this study reveals multiple young stellar populations (<100 Myr) within interstellar bubbles, with younger stars preferentially near bubble shells and older stars distributed interiorly. No clear progenitor clusters are found, suggesting low-mass clusters or OB associations drive expansion. A fundamental plane relation is established linking stellar population properties, bubble size, gas density, and feedback efficiency.
AI.motivation: To determine the demography of stellar populations within interstellar bubbles observed in JWST MIRI images and understand the role of stellar feedback in driving bubble expansion and secondary star formation.
AI.method: Resolved stellar populations (RSPs) from JWST/NIRCam images of NGC 628 (JWST-FEAST dataset) were compared with PARSEC+COLIBRI isochrones using a Bayesian framework. PHANGS-HST cluster candidates were also examined within large bubbles.
AI.result: Multiple stellar populations younger than 100 Myr are found within bubbles; youngest stars lie closer to bubble shells while older stars are distributed throughout interiors. No convincing progenitor clusters were found for large bubbles. A fundamental plane relation involving stellar mass, age, bubble size, gas density, and feedback efficiency was established.
AI.conclusion: Secondary star formation occurs within bubbles as shells expand, and low-mass clusters or OB associations may be sufficient to drive initial bubble expansion. JWST/NIRCam CMDs are effective for characterizing stellar populations driving interstellar bubble evolution in nearby galaxies.

title: Improved proper motion and gravity tests with PSR J1913+1102
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, accepted by Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: PSR J1913+1102 is a highly asymmetric double neutron star system and an excellent laboratory for testing scalar-tensor gravity theories, as well as a potential progenitor analogue of GW170817 that will merge in 470 Myr. We present an updated timing analysis combining 13 years of historical Arecibo observations and new FAST measurements, using two approaches to model dispersion-measure variations. The new timing solution provides precise measurements of four post-Keplerian parameters and improves the system mass estimates.
